claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a single-phase high-temperature BCC structure.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed primarily by competition between a composition-controlled thermodynamic driving force and diffusion-limited kinetics.
The thermodynamic driving force promotes ordering.
Ordering is accompanied by decomposition into secondary phases.
Sluggish diffusion of substitutional elements kinetically limits transformation.
Slower cooling relaxes kinetic constraints and allows transformation toward equilibrium phases.
Rapid cooling arrests phase transformations and preserves the high-temperature BCC phase.
Short-range ordered clusters or ordered precipitates nucleate from the BCC matrix during transformation.
The ordered products may have an L12 or related structure.
At high temperatures, the alloy is retained in a metastable BCC phase because diffusion rates are high at equilibrium.
On cooling, electronic and atomic-size mismatches associated with Al and the other elements produce a thermodynamic driving force for decomposition into more stable ordered phases.
Slow cooling provides sufficient time for ordering to proceed.
Slow-cooled samples will develop ordered and/or secondary phases detectable by XRD superlattice peaks and TEM precipitate observations.
Rapidly cooled samples will retain the BCC phase with minimal ordering.
The degree of ordering will correlate with the composition-dependent thermodynamic instability.
An as-cast or rapidly quenched sample provides a homogeneous BCC baseline.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply after substantial composition changes or when added alloying elements or extreme pressure alter the thermodynamic and kinetic landscapes.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says that high diffusion rates retain a metastable BCC phase at equilibrium, whereas the central hypothesis says that increased diffusional access allows transformation toward equilibrium phases. High diffusion ordinarily removes kinetic arrest rather than explaining retention of a metastable state, and describing a phase as both metastable and retained 'at equilibrium' is internally inconsistent.

The hypothesis attributes stability to competition between thermodynamic driving force and kinetic limitations, but the falsification rule reframes kinetic limitations alone as the primary governing factor. Similar cooling-rate outcomes would challenge the proposed kinetic contribution, but would not by itself falsify every version of the stated competition mechanism.
